Issued at 319 AM CDT Fri Oct 9 2026

A potent shortwave digging into the Pacific Northwest this 
morning will turn northwest flow aloft over the Northern Plains 
into low- amplitude ridging. The shortwave will also force lee 
cyclogenesis from southern Alberta to central Montana, placing 
the Dakotas under southerly return flow with strong warm air 
advection. Given very little spread in the NBM temperature 
distribution and recent observed biases, we have raised the high
temperature forecast for today to near the 75th percentile, 
giving lower 70s northeast to mid 80s southwest. The southerly 
flow will continue through tonight as the lee trough pushes 
eastward, advecting unseasonably high dewpoints in the mid 50s 
into central and eastern North Dakota. Forecast low temperatures
tonight in the upper 40s to upper 50s approach near-record warm
values.

By Saturday morning, the lee trough is projected to have 
entered western North Dakota as a cold front within a broad 
area of low pressure attendant to a deeper surface low over 
southern Saskatchewan. The cold front is projected to lie from 
the northern Red to southern James River Valleys by the end of 
the day, although some timing uncertainty is evident. The high 
temperature forecast along and ahead of the front's most likely
location at midday, roughly from the Devils Lake Basin to south
central North Dakota, was raised closer to the NBM 75th 
percentile. This gives an area-wide forecast of mid 60s 
northwest to mid and even upper 80s in the southern James River 
Valley.

The magnitude of low level cold air advection trailing the cold
front is not overly strong, but a long duration of persistent 
cooling is forecast to last through the day Sunday. The leading 
edge of the low level baroclinic zone could stall over southeast
North Dakota on Sunday, but all locations are projected to have
highs around 20 to 25 degrees colder than Saturday, ranging 
from the 40s northwest to 60s southeast. The entire NBM 
distribution has warmed slightly from previous iterations, 
which is noteworthy given increasing precipitation chances from 
Saturday night through Sunday evening driven by DCVA, a split 
upper jet, and transient low to mid level frontogenesis. 
Ensemble mean QPF and threshold probabilities have slightly 
decreased and slightly shifted northward compared to previous 
forecasts. Through Sunday evening, a triangular area of 50 
percent or greater chances of at least a tenth of an inch of 
rain is generally enclosed by a line from the southwest to 
northeast corners of the state and the Montana and Canadian 
borders. Confidence that temperatures will remain above 
freezing over this time period is very high.

Most guidance shows a brief break in precipitation chances late
Sunday evening before another wave of DCVA ejects from the base
of a western CONUS trough. Previous forecasts had noted strong 
jet dynamics with this second round of DCVA, but recent 
deterministic models now favor the left exit region of the 
southern jet streak to remain much further south. There is still
sufficient forcing for ascent to produce widespread 
precipitation late Sunday night through Monday, and transient 
mid level frontogenesis could enhance precipitation rates at 
times. The NBM places at least a 40 percent chance for exceeding
a tenth of an inch of QPF over all but southeast North Dakota, 
which lines up well with 2 ensemble clusters that are comprised 
of two thirds of the total global ensemble membership. The 
highest QPF probabilities (around 60-80% for exceeding 0.1" and 
40-60% for exceeding 0.25") are placed over western North 
Dakota, but clusters reveal north-to-south uncertainty where the
highest amounts could fall. The slight warming trend of the NBM
temperature distribution is carried through Monday, with Sunday
night lows now forecast to remain above freezing at most 
locations. Given this combined with slightly weaker forcing 
lowering the dynamic cooling potential, the probability for snow
has greatly diminished. There could still be a brief rain/snow 
mix in western parts of the state early Monday morning, but the 
probability of just a tenth of an inch of snow has fallen to no 
greater than 10 percent.

The high temperature forecast on Monday has risen slightly, but
still remains below normal at around 45 to 50. There is 
uncertainty on how quickly rain will diminish, which could be 
as early as late Monday afternoon or as late as early Tuesday 
morning in some locations. This could have great implications 
on the Monday night low temperature forecast, as any areas that 
become cloud free will be very likely to see below freezing 
temperatures. Lows could still approach freezing even underneath
cloud cover, but there is still very little to no chance of any
lingering precipitation changing over to snow.
